more.title: The alliance is unravelling, heralding a new era for politics
more.description: The SACP’s decision to contest the upcoming local government elections independently of the ANC is more than a political disagreement; it is a tectonic shift. With the polls two months away, the move signals the end of the tripartite alliance as a functional governing force. The political and ideological threads that have bound the movements since the struggle against apartheid are now irreparably frayed. For decades, the SACP, the ANC and Cosatu operated as a “strategic” unit, with the SACP acting as the intellectual and ideological engine room. This often resulted in the SACP wielding significant influence over policy without having to account for its performance at the ballot box. By severing the link and standing independently, the SACP is gambling that its ideological purity and grassroots organisation will resonate with a disillusioned electorate, even as it risks splitting the alliance’s voter base. The schism could reshape politics. The ANC is in a precarious governing coalition in which it and the DA are the dominant partners. This has not gone down well with the SACP leadership, hence the severing of electoral ties. The SACP’s independent campaign will force the ANC to contend with a competitor that understands its internal machinery but offers a more radical, state-centric economic alternative. This could push the ANC back towards its centrist, market-accommodating instincts to differentiate itself from the Left. The coming weeks are expected to see fierce debates over issues such as land expropriation and fiscal discipline as electoral weapons; instead of just a narrow focus on service delivery concerns. The collapse of the alliance will also alter the mechanics of coalition politics. In the upcoming elections, neither the ANC nor the SACP is expected to achieve an outright majority in key metropolitan areas. The ideological kinship between the two, however, suggests they may be forced to enter into a coalition arrangement with each other or other parties, depending on how well the SACP does. Sceptics expect it to fare badly but we can’t rule it out as possible kingmaker. If the ANC chooses to approach the EFF or the uMkhonto weSizwe Party for possible post-electoral pacts, it could push the SACP into permanent opposition, creating a split in the liberation movement vote that could lead to political gridlock. The electorate has a desire for accountability and service delivery, which the alliance structure often obscured. By forcing parties to stand on their own records, voters may finally be able to choose a clear ideological path. The disappearance of the alliance umbrella means no party can hide behind the collective history of the struggle; they must stand or fall on their governance track record. Ultimately, the 2026 local government elections will no longer be a mere gauge of ANC support but a moment that determines whether South Africa moves towards a more ideologically polarised governance structure or descends into political fragmentation.

more.title: Ruthless All Blacks punish wasteful Boks
more.description: There are rugby matches and then there is Springboks versus All Blacks. At Ellis Park last night, Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry turned into a black-and-blue ambush as New Zealand delivered a thunderous 33-16 victory, leaving the world champions with more questions than answers. The All Blacks scored five tries to one, exposing a fatal flaw in the Springbok game: enormous pressure without enough attacking polish. For 40 minutes, the Boks looked every inch the heavyweight contenders. Their scrum became a demolition site, their maul a runaway locomotive and their forwards battered the All Blacks across the park. Yet New Zealand had the scoreboard. Will Jordan, Josh Moorby, Fabian Holland, Luke Jacobson and Jordan again crossed for the visitors, while Ruben Love converted four tries. Jordan’s second score in the 75th minute applied the final coat of black paint to a bruising victory. South Africa’s points came from Cheslin Kolbe’s two penalties in the first half and two in the second, plus a converted try from replacement André Esterhuizen. Kolbe finished with 11 points, while Esterhuizen’s five-pointer briefly appeared to have tilted the contest towards the hosts. At half-time, the Boks led 13-12, despite New Zealand having crossed twice. That scoreline flattered South Africa’s execution. The Boks repeatedly marched into the All Blacks’ red zone and returned empty-handed. Malcolm Marx lost possession over the line, while a succession of promising attacking movements dissolved into dropped passes, loose handling and ponderous decision-making. New Zealand played like street fighters with silk gloves. Ruben Love, Cam Roigard and Damian McKenzie supplied the creative spark, while Ardie Savea prowled like a shark smelling blood. The All Blacks needed little invitation to turn scraps into scoring opportunities. Fabian Holland’s charge-down try early in the second half was the dagger. Luke Jacobson’s score stretched the wound, before Jordan’s late double finished the job. The Boks’ scrum remained magnificent. Their attack remained maddening. That was the cruel arithmetic of the evening. Even Damian de Allende’s 100th Test cap could not rescue South Africa from an All Blacks side that defended with ferocity and attacked with ruthless clarity. Two late yellow cards for Cobus Reinach and Marco van Staden compounded the misery. New Zealand have drawn first blood. Now the rivalry moves to DHL Stadium in Cape Town on Saturday, where the Boks must find a sharper edge or risk watching the All Blacks run away with the series. Ellis Park belonged to the visitors. Cape Town awaits the reply.
